name: go-agent-skills
description: Curated Go skills for code review, concurrency, testing, and architecture
readme:
Curated Go skills for AI coding agents.
Idiomatic by default, loaded only when they matter.

Quick start · Usage · Skills · How it works · Evaluations · Customizing · FAQ · Contributing

```bash npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills ``` --- ## Why AI coding agents write Go that compiles. Writing Go that reads like Go takes more than that. Left to defaults, an agent returns errors with no context, declares interfaces next to their only implementation, starts goroutines nothing ever stops, and reaches for `interface{}` where a type parameter belongs. **go-agent-skills** gives the agent the judgment an experienced Go reviewer brings: 35 focused skills grounded in [Effective Go](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go), [Go Code Review Comments](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments), and patterns from large-scale production Go services. They follow the open [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/) standard, work in any compatible agent, and load **on demand**. Until a skill is relevant, it costs about 135 tokens. ```go // ❌ Before: the caller gets "sql: no rows in result set" and nothing else func (s *Service) User(id int) (*User, error) { u, err := s.repo.Find(id) if err != nil { return nil, err } return u, nil } // ✅ After (go-error-handling + go-context): cancellable, wrapped, still matchable func (s *Service) User(ctx context.Context, id int) (*User, error) { u, err := s.repo.Find(ctx, id) if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("find user %d: %w", id, err) } return u, nil } ``` ### Highlights - 🎯 **35 skills across six areas.** Code quality, architecture, data, safety and performance, testing, and workflow. - 🪶 **Progressive disclosure.** About 4,800 tokens of descriptions at startup. Bodies and 62 reference files load only when a task needs them. - 🧭 **A router for overlap.** `go-skills-router` maps a task to the skill that owns it and draws the line where two overlap. - 🧪 **Measured, not asserted.** 159 eval cases you run with and without the skills. The difference between the two runs is the result. - 🔐 **Least privilege.** Every skill declares scoped `allowed-tools`. Review and audit skills cannot write. - 🔄 **Current with Go.** Covers Go 1.21 through 1.27. A weekly workflow opens an issue when a new Go release ships that `go-modernize` doesn't cover yet. - 🔌 **Agent-agnostic.** Works in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, OpenCode, Cline, and more. --- ## 🚀 Quick start Install with the [`npx skills`](https://skills.sh) CLI. It detects the agents you have and puts each skill where that agent looks for it. That covers **Claude Code**, **Cursor**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Windsurf**, **OpenCode**, **Cline**, and [37+ more agents](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills#available-agents). ```bash # Everything, interactive npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills # Look before you install npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills --list # Only the skills you want npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills --skill go-code-review --skill go-defensive-coding # Globally, for every project npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills -g # Non-interactive, for CI and dotfiles npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills --all -y ```
Claude Code: plugin marketplace ```bash /plugin marketplace add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills /plugin install go-agent-skills@eduardo-sl ``` Or install the files directly: `npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills -a claude-code`
Cursor ```bash npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills -a cursor ``` Cursor auto-discovers skills from `.cursor/skills/` and `.agents/skills/`.
GitHub Copilot ```bash npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills -a copilot ``` Copilot auto-discovers skills from `.github/skills/`.
Codex ```bash npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills -a codex ``` Codex auto-discovers skills from `~/.agents/skills/` and `.agents/skills/`.
Windsurf · OpenCode · Cline ```bash npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills -a windsurf npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills -a opencode npx skills add eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills -a cline ```
Shell installer: no Node required ```bash git clone https://github.com/eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills.git ./go-agent-skills/scripts/install.sh /path/to/your-go-project --agent claude # Preview without changing anything ./go-agent-skills/scripts/install.sh /path/to/project --agent claude --dry-run # Symlink instead of copying, so a `git pull` updates every project ./go-agent-skills/scripts/install.sh /path/to/project --agent claude --symlink ``` Agents: `claude`, `cursor`, `copilot`, `codex`, `windsurf`. Add `--global` to install into your home directory.
Manual copy ```bash mkdir -p .claude/skills && cp -r go-agent-skills/skills/*/* .claude/skills/ # Claude Code mkdir -p .cursor/skills && cp -r go-agent-skills/skills/*/* .cursor/skills/ # Cursor mkdir -p .github/skills && cp -r go-agent-skills/skills/*/* .github/skills/ # Copilot mkdir -p .agents/skills && cp -r go-agent-skills/skills/*/* .agents/skills/ # Codex / OpenCode ```
Keeping them up to date ```bash npx skills check # anything out of date? npx skills update # bring them current npx skills list # what is installed npx skills remove go-performance-review ```
--- ## 💬 Usage There is nothing to learn. Work as usual, and the agent loads a skill when your task matches its description. Agents that support slash commands can also invoke a skill directly: ```text /go-code-review /go-concurrency-review ``` Real tasks usually need more than one skill. These combinations come from [`go-skills-router`](skills/(workflow)/go-skills-router/): | Ask your agent | Skills it loads | | --- | --- | | "Review this PR" | `go-code-review` | | "Build a gRPC service with tests" | `go-grpc` + `go-test-quality` + `go-error-handling` | | "This endpoint is slow under load" | `go-troubleshooting` + `go-performance-review` + `go-database` | | "Harden this service before launch" | `go-security-audit` + `go-dependency-audit` + `go-defensive-coding` + `go-ci` | | "Split this monolith" | `go-architecture-review` + `go-refactoring` + `go-semantic-tools` | | "Scaffold a new CLI" | `go-project-layout` + `go-cli` + `go-ci` + `go-binary-size` | | "Migrate this to the current Go release" | `go-modernize` + `go-test-quality` + `go-ci` | > [!TIP] > To make a project use the skills on every Go task, ask your agent to > **"set up the Go skills for this repo"**. `go-skills-router` proposes a short > block for your `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, or Copilot/Cursor rules, and writes it > only after you approve the diff. --- ## 🧩 Skills ```text ┌──────────────────┐ │ go-skills-router │ ← which skill owns this task? owns it, plus the secondary skills to load | "which skill should I use", "what Go skills do you have" | 175 | 2,657 | 2,657 | --- ## 🧠 How it works Each skill loads in three tiers, and each tier is paid for only when it is needed: ```text always loaded when a task matches when the skill points there ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ description │ ─────▶ │ SKILL.md │ ─────▶ │ references/*.md │ │ what it covers, │ │ procedure, good/bad │ │ edge cases, recipes, │ │ when NOT to fire │ │ pairs, checklist │ │ migrations │ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────────┘ └────────────────────────┘ ~135 tokens each ~2,000 tokens each never all at once ~4,800 for all 35 2–4 per typical task ~125,000 in the full tree ``` The descriptions are the only cost paid on every request, Go work or not. A typical task fires two to four skills. The full tree is about 26 times the startup cost and is never loaded at once. That gap is the point of progressive disclosure. --- ## 🧪 Evaluations A skill that doesn't change the output costs context for nothing. [`evals/`](evals/) is the harness that tells the difference: 159 cases, each a realistic prompt with regex assertions and optional rubric checks graded by a second model. ```bash # In a project with the skills installed scripts/run-evals.py --cmd 'claude -p "{prompt}"' --label with-skills # In one without them scripts/run-evals.py --cmd 'claude -p "{prompt}"' --label baseline ``` The delta is the measurement. `--cmd` takes any agent CLI, so the same suite runs against whatever agent you use. One suite measures something different. `go-skills-router` asserts *which skill* a task should route to. With 35 skills whose triggers overlap, routing to the wrong one costs more than any description does. The case format is documented in [`evals/README.md`](evals/README.md). > [!NOTE] > No scores are published here. Results depend on the model, its version, and > the day you run them, and a score without those three recorded tells you > nothing. Run the suite against your own agent and judge for yourself. --- ## 🔐 Security Skills are prompts injected into an agent that already has shell and file-write access. This repository treats them as security-sensitive: - **Least-privilege tools.** Every skill declares `allowed-tools`. Review and audit skills cannot write, and every `Bash(...)` grant is scoped to one binary. - **No remote code.** No skill fetches remote content or runs downloaded code. The only external hosts referenced anywhere in `skills/` are `github.com` and `localhost`. - **Enforced in CI.** `scripts/validate.sh` rejects unscoped `Bash`, any skill that declares itself read-only but asks for `Write`, and any instruction that pipes a download into a shell. - **Scanned on publish.** [skills.sh](https://www.skills.sh/eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills) scans every published skill with Socket, Snyk, and Gen Agent Trust Hub. The threat model and private disclosure process are in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). --- ## 🎚 Customizing **Your team's conventions win.** The convention skills (`go-coding-standards`, `go-error-handling`, `go-test-quality`, `go-api-design`, `go-database`, `git-commit`, and others) are marked as community defaults. To override one without forking, write a short team skill, or a rule in `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, that names the skill it supersedes: ```markdown This skill supersedes `go-coding-standards` for Acme projects. ``` Where the two disagree, the agent follows yours. For deeper changes, fork the repository and install from your fork with `npx skills add your-org/go-agent-skills`. **Fixing triggers.** If a skill fires too often, or doesn't fire when it should, the fix is its `description` field, because that field is the entire triggering mechanism. [Open an issue](https://github.com/eduardo-sl/go-agent-skills/issues) with the prompt that misrouted and the skill you expected. Small wording changes have a large effect on trigger accuracy. --- ## 🎯 Design principles - **Written for agents, not readers.** Imperative steps, ✅/❌ contrast pairs, and a verification checklist at the end of every skill. Agents learn from contrast, not prose. - **Negative triggers earn their keep.** Every description says what the skill does *not* cover and names the skill that does. Loading the wrong skill costs more than loading none. - **Verification is executable.** Where a tool can prove a rule (`go vet`, `golangci-lint`, `govulncheck`, `go test -race`), the skill runs that tool instead of asking the agent to judge. - **Small by default.** `SKILL.md` stays within 250 lines. CI warns above that and fails above 500. Depth goes in `references/`. - **Self-contained.** No skill requires another to be loaded first. Skills name each other only as pointers. `go-skills-router` is the one index, and it is optional too. --- ## 🧱 Repository structure ```text go-agent-skills/ ├── skills/(category)/skill-name/ │ ├── SKILL.md # ≤250 lines: procedure, patterns, checklist │ └── references/ # depth, loaded only when SKILL.md says so ├── evals/ │ ├── README.md # how to measure a skill's worth │ └── cases/ # one prompt + assertion suite per skill ├── scripts/ │ ├── install.sh # shell installer (--dry-run, --symlink) │ ├── run-evals.py # drives any agent CLI │ ├── validate.sh # format, frontmatter, tools, catalogue sync │ └── check-go-release.sh # flags Go releases go-modernize doesn't cover ├── docs/ │ ├── SKILL_GUIDELINES.md # quality bar for authoring │ └── skill-gap-analysis.md # what exists, what was rejected, and why │ │ # platform discovery files: all must list the same skills ├── AGENTS.md · CLAUDE.md · .claude-plugin/marketplace.json ├── .cursor/rules/ · .windsurf/rules/ · .clinerules · .github/copilot-instructions.md └── .opencode/config.json ``` --- ## ❓ FAQ
Do the skills cost anything when I'm not writing Go? Only the descriptions, about 4,800 tokens for all 35. Skill bodies load only when a task matches. To cut that further, install only the skills you use (`--skill`) or install per project instead of globally.
Do I need all 35? No. Every skill is self-contained and works alone. A good starting set is `go-code-review`, `go-error-handling`, `go-concurrency-review`, and `go-test-quality`. Add more as your tasks need them.
Which Go versions are covered? Go 1.21 through 1.27. Advice that depends on a release is labeled with it (for example, `sync.WaitGroup.Go`, *Go 1.25+*), so the agent checks `go.mod` before suggesting it. A weekly workflow opens an issue when a new Go release ships that `go-modernize` doesn't cover yet.
Is this only for Claude Code? No. The skills follow the open [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/) standard and contain no agent-specific instructions. The repository also ships discovery files for Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, Cline, and OpenCode, and CI checks that they list every skill.
Can a skill run commands on my machine? A skill runs nothing by itself. It steers your agent, and it declares the tools it needs in `allowed-tools`. Some agents pre-approve those tools while the skill is active, so the grants are kept narrow. Review and audit skills are read-only, and every `Bash` grant is scoped to a single binary such as `go` or `gofmt`. See [Security](#-security).
--- ## 🤝 Contributing Contributions are welcome. The skills are loaded into agents that real engineers use on real codebases, so a small, correct contribution is worth more than a large one. Good places to start: - **A misrouted prompt.** Open an issue with what you typed and the skill you expected. - **An eval case.** Add a case that fails without the skill and passes with it. - **A factual fix.** Wrong API, outdated Go version, or an example that doesn't compile. - **A new skill.** Check [`docs/skill-gap-analysis.md`](docs/skill-gap-analysis.md) first. It lists what has been considered and why. The budget for each skill: | | Target | | --- | --- | | `description` | ~100–200 tokens: what it does, when to fire, when *not* to | | `SKILL.md` | ≤250 lines, ~1,000–2,000 tokens: procedure and patterns, nothing else | | `references/*.md` | Whatever depth needs, loaded on demand | | Full tree | Under ~10,000 tokens | Every PR must pass `./scripts/validate.sh` and ship at least one eval case that fails without the skill. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [docs/SKILL_GUIDELINES.md](docs/SKILL_GUIDELINES.md) before opening one. --- ## 🙏 Acknowledgements - [Effective Go](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go): the Go team's guide to idiomatic Go - [Go Code Review Comments](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments): the community's review standards - [Uber Go Style Guide](https://github.com/uber-go/guide/blob/master/style.md): cited where a convention comes from it - [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/): the open skill specification - [Vercel Skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills): the `npx skills` distribution ecosystem - [Anthropic Skills](https://github.com/anthropics/skills): patterns for production-grade skills The Go gopher was designed by [Renée French](https://reneefrench.blogspot.com/) and is licensed under [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/). ---

Why

AI coding agents write Go that compiles. Writing Go that reads like Go takes

more than that. Left to defaults, an agent returns errors with no context,

declares interfaces next to their only implementation, starts goroutines nothing

ever stops, and reaches for interface{} where a type parameter belongs.

go-agent-skills gives the agent the judgment an experienced Go reviewer

brings: 35 focused skills grounded in Effective Go,

Go Code Review Comments, and patterns

from large-scale production Go services. They follow the open

Agent Skills standard, work in any compatible agent,

and load on demand. Until a skill is relevant, it costs about 135 tokens.


// ❌ Before: the caller gets "sql: no rows in result set" and nothing else

func (s *Service) User(id int) (*User, error) {

    u, err := s.repo.Find(id)

    if err != nil {

        return nil, err

    }

    return u, nil

}



// ✅ After (go-error-handling + go-context): cancellable, wrapped, still matchable

func (s *Service) User(ctx context.Context, id int) (*User, error) {

    u, err := s.repo.Find(ctx, id)

    if err != nil {

        return nil, fmt.Errorf("find user %d: %w", id, err)

    }

    return u, nil

}

Highlights

  • 🎯 35 skills across six areas. Code quality, architecture, data, safety and performance, testing, and workflow.
  • 🪶 Progressive disclosure. About 4,800 tokens of descriptions at startup. Bodies and 62 reference files load only when a task needs them.
  • 🧭 A router for overlap. go-skills-router maps a task to the skill that owns it and draws the line where two overlap.
  • 🧪 Measured, not asserted. 159 eval cases you run with and without the skills. The difference between the two runs is the result.
  • 🔐 Least privilege. Every skill declares scoped allowed-tools. Review and audit skills cannot write.
  • 🔄 Current with Go. Covers Go 1.21 through 1.27. A weekly workflow opens an issue when a new Go release ships that go-modernize doesn't cover yet.
  • 🔌 Agent-agnostic. Works in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, OpenCode, Cline, and more.

💬 Usage

There is nothing to learn. Work as usual, and the agent loads a skill when your

task matches its description. Agents that support slash commands can also

invoke a skill directly:


/go-code-review

/go-concurrency-review

Real tasks usually need more than one skill. These combinations come from

[go-skills-router](skills/(workflow)/go-skills-router/):

| Ask your agent | Skills it loads |

| --- | --- |

| "Review this PR" | go-code-review |

| "Build a gRPC service with tests" | go-grpc + go-test-quality + go-error-handling |

| "This endpoint is slow under load" | go-troubleshooting + go-performance-review + go-database |

| "Harden this service before launch" | go-security-audit + go-dependency-audit + go-defensive-coding + go-ci |

| "Split this monolith" | go-architecture-review + go-refactoring + go-semantic-tools |

| "Scaffold a new CLI" | go-project-layout + go-cli + go-ci + go-binary-size |

> To make a project use the skills on every Go task, ask your agent to

🧠 How it works

Each skill loads in three tiers, and each tier is paid for only when it is needed:


    always loaded             when a task matches            when the skill points there

┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────┐

│   description    │ ─────▶ │       SKILL.md       │ ─────▶ │    references/*.md     │

│ what it covers,  │        │ procedure, good/bad  │        │ edge cases, recipes,   │

│ when NOT to fire │        │ pairs, checklist     │        │ migrations             │

└──────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────┘

  ~135 tokens each            ~2,000 tokens each              never all at once

  ~4,800 for all 35           2–4 per typical task            ~125,000 in the full tree

The descriptions are the only cost paid on every request, Go work or not. A

typical task fires two to four skills. The full tree is about 26 times the

startup cost and is never loaded at once. That gap is the point of

progressive disclosure.

🧪 Evaluations

A skill that doesn't change the output costs context for nothing.

[evals/](evals/) is the harness that tells the difference: 159 cases, each a

realistic prompt with regex assertions and optional rubric checks graded by a

second model.


# In a project with the skills installed

scripts/run-evals.py --cmd 'claude -p "{prompt}"' --label with-skills



# In one without them

scripts/run-evals.py --cmd 'claude -p "{prompt}"' --label baseline

The delta is the measurement. --cmd takes any agent CLI, so the same suite

runs against whatever agent you use.

One suite measures something different. go-skills-router asserts *which

skill* a task should route to. With 35 skills whose triggers overlap, routing

to the wrong one costs more than any description does. The case format is

documented in [evals/README.md](evals/README.md).

> [!NOTE]

> No scores are published here. Results depend on the model, its version, and

> the day you run them, and a score without those three recorded tells you

> nothing. Run the suite against your own agent and judge for yourself.

🔐 Security

Skills are prompts injected into an agent that already has shell and file-write

access. This repository treats them as security-sensitive:

  • Least-privilege tools. Every skill declares allowed-tools. Review and

audit skills cannot write, and every Bash(...) grant is scoped to one binary.

  • No remote code. No skill fetches remote content or runs downloaded code.

The only external hosts referenced anywhere in skills/ are github.com and

localhost.

  • Enforced in CI. scripts/validate.sh rejects unscoped Bash, any skill

that declares itself read-only but asks for Write, and any instruction that

pipes a download into a shell.

  • Scanned on publish. skills.sh

scans every published skill with Socket, Snyk, and Gen Agent Trust Hub.

The threat model and private disclosure process are in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

🎚 Customizing

Your team's conventions win. The convention skills (go-coding-standards,

go-error-handling, go-test-quality, go-api-design, go-database,

git-commit, and others) are marked as community defaults. To override one

without forking, write a short team skill, or a rule in CLAUDE.md or

AGENTS.md, that names the skill it supersedes:


This skill supersedes `go-coding-standards` for Acme projects.

Where the two disagree, the agent follows yours. For deeper changes, fork the

repository and install from your fork with

npx skills add your-org/go-agent-skills.

Fixing triggers. If a skill fires too often, or doesn't fire when it should,

the fix is its description field, because that field is the entire triggering

mechanism. Open an issue

with the prompt that misrouted and the skill you expected. Small wording changes

have a large effect on trigger accuracy.

---

🎯 Design principles

  • Written for agents, not readers. Imperative steps, ✅/❌ contrast pairs,

and a verification checklist at the end of every skill. Agents learn from

contrast, not prose.

  • Negative triggers earn their keep. Every description says what the skill

does *not* cover and names the skill that does. Loading the wrong skill costs

more than loading none.

  • Verification is executable. Where a tool can prove a rule (go vet,

golangci-lint, govulncheck, go test -race), the skill runs that tool

instead of asking the agent to judge.

  • Small by default. SKILL.md stays within 250 lines. CI warns above that

and fails above 500. Depth goes in references/.

  • Self-contained. No skill requires another to be loaded first. Skills name

each other only as pointers. go-skills-router is the one index, and it is

optional too.

❓ FAQ

<details>

<summary><b>Do the skills cost anything when I'm not writing Go?</b></summary>

Only the descriptions, about 4,800 tokens for all 35. Skill bodies load only

when a task matches. To cut that further, install only the skills you use

(--skill) or install per project instead of globally.

</details>

<details>

<summary><b>Do I need all 35?</b></summary>

No. Every skill is self-contained and works alone. A good starting set is

go-code-review, go-error-handling, go-concurrency-review, and

go-test-quality. Add more as your tasks need them.

</details>

<details>

<summary><b>Which Go versions are covered?</b></summary>

Go 1.21 through 1.27. Advice that depends on a release is labeled with it

(for example, sync.WaitGroup.Go, *Go 1.25+*), so the agent checks go.mod

before suggesting it. A weekly workflow opens an issue when a new Go release

ships that go-modernize doesn't cover yet.

</details>

<details>

<summary><b>Is this only for Claude Code?</b></summary>

No. The skills follow the open Agent Skills standard

and contain no agent-specific instructions. The repository also ships discovery

files for Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, Cline, and OpenCode, and CI checks that they

list every skill.

</details>

<details>

<summary><b>Can a skill run commands on my machine?</b></summary>

A skill runs nothing by itself. It steers your agent, and it declares the tools it

needs in allowed-tools. Some agents pre-approve those tools while the skill is

active, so the grants are kept narrow. Review and audit skills are read-only, and

every Bash grant is scoped to a single binary such as go or gofmt. See

[Security](#-security).

</details>

than a large one. Good places to start:

  • A misrouted prompt. Open an issue with what you typed and the skill you expected.
  • An eval case. Add a case that fails without the skill and passes with it.
  • A factual fix. Wrong API, outdated Go version, or an example that doesn't compile.
  • A new skill. Check [docs/skill-gap-analysis.md](docs/skill-gap-analysis.md) first. It lists what has been considered and why.

The budget for each skill:

| | Target |

| --- | --- |

| description | ~100–200 tokens: what it does, when to fire, when *not* to |

| SKILL.md | ≤250 lines, ~1,000–2,000 tokens: procedure and patterns, nothing else |

| references/*.md | Whatever depth needs, loaded on demand |

| Full tree | Under ~10,000 tokens |

Every PR must pass ./scripts/validate.sh and ship at least one eval case that

fails without the skill. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and

[docs/SKILL_GUIDELINES.md](docs/SKILL_GUIDELINES.md) before opening one.
